ledger.explanation:
Dockerd requires the unprivileged user namespace element (ns.userns_unpriv) to create isolated user namespaces for containers, mapping container UID/GID ranges to the host and enabling rootless or multi‑tenant containers without granting them real host privileges. This isolation prevents uid collisions and confines a compromised container to its own namespace.  

From this surface an attacker gains a user‑namespace escape primitive (netfilter‑via‑userns or userns‑lpe) for host privilege escalation, an io_uring refcount use‑after‑free primitive allowing arbitrary kernel memory read/write, an io_uring use‑after‑free primitive with similar effect, a keyring use‑after‑free primitive that leaks or overwrites credential objects, and a keyctl refcount‑overflow primitive that corrupts reference counts leading to memory‑corruption‑based code execution.  

Disable unprivileged user namespaces for dockerd, e.g., start it with --userns-remap=disabled or set kernel.user.max_user_namespaces=0, which removes ns.userns_unpriv usage. The tradeoff is that containers run in the host’s UID/GID namespace, losing uid/gid isolation and increasing the impact of any container breakout on the host.

libvirtd runs as root and opens /dev/kvm to issue KVM ioctls that create virtual machines, allocate vCPUs, set up memory regions, and control device assignment. Without this devnode the daemon cannot access hardware‑assisted virtualization, so the sole‑owner element dev.kvm is required for its core workflow.

An attacker who can influence libvirtd’s KVM ioctl input can trigger an out‑of‑bounds write in the kvm ioctl handler, achieving arbitrary kernel memory corruption. This primitive yields privilege escalation from the libvirtd process (uid 0) to full kernel code execution, as reflected in the kvm‑ioctl CVE cluster.

The surface can be removed by disabling KVM acceleration in libvirtd/QEMU and letting QEMU use its TCG software emulator instead of /dev/kvm. This preserves the ability to start and manage VMs but incurs substantial CPU overhead, slowing guest execution and increasing host load.

The workload has no sole‑owner elements, so there is no function that uniquely requires any such element. The surface remains open because nginx shares the io_uring setup syscall (sc.io_uring_setup) to perform asynchronous I/O for high‑speed network traffic.  

An attacker who can reach this shared element gains two exploitation primitives: the ability to manipulate io_uring reference counts (leading to overflow or underflow) and to trigger a use‑after‑free condition in the io_uring subsystem. These primitives allow arbitrary kernel memory read/write and privilege escalation.  

The surface can be removed by disabling nginx’s use of io_uring, for example by setting `use io_uring off;` in the nginx configuration or by building nginx without the io_uring module and relying on its default epoll event loop. This preserves the ability to serve HTTP requests while eliminating the sc.io_uring_setup exposure, though it reduces the asynchronous I/O throughput that io_uring provides.

udisksd runs as root to automatically detect and mount block devices. It needs the usb_storage kernel module to enumerate USB mass‑storage devices, expose them as /dev/sd* nodes, and trigger its automount policies. Without this module it cannot see USB sticks, so the workload keeps the surface open to provide transparent USB storage handling.

The usb_storage module (weight 4.5) links to one reachable CVE in the usb‑parsing cluster. Exploiting this flaw triggers a heap‑based buffer overflow when parsing malicious USB device descriptors, giving an attacker arbitrary kernel code execution and privilege escalation from user space to root.

Add a udev rule that sets ENV{UDISKS_IGNORE}=1 for all USB storage devices; udisksd will skip probing them, allowing the usb_storage module to be unloaded while udisks2 still handles optical discs or other block devices. If automatic USB mounting is required, no substitute exists and the trade‑off is loss of that automation, requiring manual mount or a less privileged userspace mounter.

The workload w.sshd has no sole‑owner elements, so the only reason the attack surface remains open is its use of the shared element sc.keyctl. sshd invokes the keyctl syscall to manage kernel keyrings for storing authentication tokens and session keys.  

Through sc.keyctl an attacker can trigger a use‑after‑free on keyring objects and a reference‑count overflow, giving the primitives of arbitrary kernel memory read/write and privilege escalation via corrupted keyring references.  

If the operator does not need keyring‑based authentication, they can disable the feature in sshd (e.g., turn off GSSAPIKeyExchange or apply a seccomp filter that blocks keyctl) which removes the surface; otherwise the surface must be retained because sshd’s workflow depends on keyctl for its keyring operations.
